meta.disclaimer: Food traditions vary by region, family and cook. Dietary labels below are planning prompts, not guarantees: always confirm ingredients, cooking stock and cross-contact directly.

countries.name: Namibia
countries.lead: Build a food day around Windhoek markets, coastal seafood and the distinct cooking traditions of northern Namibia.
countries.dietaryNote: Meat is prominent in many well-known dishes. Ask for mahangu or maize porridge, beans and greens without meat stock; packaged spice mixes and relishes need checking.
ask: Was this cooked with meat stock?
Is the relish made with peanuts or another nut?

countries.name: South Africa
countries.lead: Treat the country as many food regions: Cape Malay kitchens, township food businesses, braai culture, Indian Ocean flavours and the Winelands.
countries.dietaryNote: Large cities usually offer the widest choice. Halaal certification and kitchen separation vary, so ask the venue; curries, chutneys and baked goods may contain nuts, dairy or gluten.
ask: Is the venue Halaal-certified or simply pork-free?
Does the vegetable dish contain ghee, butter or meat stock?

source.label: South African Tourism — food and wine

countries.name: Botswana
countries.lead: Use Gaborone and Maun for wider choice, then ask lodges and community hosts about regional Setwana dishes and local sourcing.
countries.dietaryNote: Maize or sorghum staples can suit some gluten-aware travellers, but shared kitchens and sauces still need checking. Vegetarian plates may require advance notice at remote camps.
ask: Can the vegetables be cooked without meat stock?
What food can I buy before the next remote leg?

source.label: Botswana Tourism — Ghanzi and local food resources

countries.name: Zambia
countries.lead: Start with nshima and its relishes, then compare market, city and lodge interpretations rather than hunting for one definitive plate.
foods: Nshima with vegetable or meat relishes
countries.dietaryNote: Plant-based relishes are common possibilities, but groundnuts and cooking stock are important questions. Nshima is maize-based; cross-contact is still kitchen-specific.
ask: Which relishes are made without meat, fish or stock?

countries.name: Zimbabwe
countries.lead: Pair sadza with locally available relishes, and leave room for regional produce, tea and street or home-style cooking along the route.
countries.dietaryNote: Sadza is maize-based, but the relish determines the meal. Peanut butter is used in some greens and sauces; ask about stock, dairy and shared utensils.
ask: Is the muriwo cooked with peanut butter?
Can I have a vegetable relish without meat stock?

countries.name: Mozambique
countries.lead: Follow the coast through seafood, coconut, cassava leaves and piri-piri, while inland tables bring different staples and preparations.
countries.dietaryNote: Matapa may include groundnuts, coconut and sometimes seafood; confirm the recipe. Grills and sauces can share utensils, and coastal availability changes with season and catch.
ask: Does the matapa contain peanuts or seafood?
Was this grilled separately from shellfish?

countries.name: Malawi
countries.lead: Connect market produce, highland tea country and Lake Malawi, while choosing lake fish with current sustainability advice in mind.
countries.dietaryNote: Vegetable ndiwo can be adaptable, but groundnuts and fish may be present. Ask before ordering and seek current local guidance before choosing threatened fish species.
ask: Does the ndiwo contain fish, meat stock or groundnuts?
Which locally caught fish is the more sustainable choice today?

countries.name: Lesotho
countries.lead: Highland food planning is about warmth, seasonality and advance communication with rural stays more than a long restaurant list.
countries.dietaryNote: Simple maize, sorghum, bean and vegetable dishes may be adaptable. Remote stays can have limited supplies, so communicate dietary needs before arrival.
ask: Can you prepare the vegetables without meat stock?
Should I bring any specialist food from Maseru?

countries.name: Eswatini
countries.lead: Link the central craft-and-food corridor with local produce, fair-trade pantry goods and food events that put Swati makers first.
countries.dietaryNote: Craft centres and city restaurants can broaden options, but dairy and shared preparation are common questions. Ask producers directly about ingredients in preserves and sauces.
ask: Does this contain emasi, milk or butter?
Which products are made by local or fair-trade producers?

routeIdeas.title: Cape kitchens to the Garden Route
routeIdeas.summary: Use Cape Town for Cape Malay and city food stories, add a Winelands day with a sober driver, then follow seasonal producers east.
routeIdeas.note: Pre-book small-group or community-led experiences; never combine wine tasting with driving.

routeIdeas.title: Maputo to the Inhambane table
routeIdeas.summary: Begin with Maputo’s markets and grills, then follow coconut, cassava-leaf and seafood traditions north toward the lagoons.
routeIdeas.note: Ask about the day’s catch, shellfish cross-contact and road conditions before each leg.

routeIdeas.title: Tea country to Lake Malawi
routeIdeas.summary: Connect arranged tea-estate visits with southern markets, highland produce and lake communities on a slower wildlife-and-food circuit.
routeIdeas.note: Confirm estate access and seek current sustainability guidance before ordering lake fish.

routeIdeas.title: Windhoek, coast and northern staples
routeIdeas.summary: Compare Windhoek’s kapana culture with Atlantic seafood and the mahangu-based food traditions encountered farther north.
routeIdeas.note: Treat markets as working places: ask before photographing, sampling or filming vendors.

etiquette.title: Ask before the camera
etiquette.text: Markets and kitchens are workplaces. Ask the person—not only a guide—before photographing people, stalls or food preparation.

etiquette.title: Agree before ordering
etiquette.text: Confirm the dish, portion, price and payment method before food is prepared, especially where menus are informal.

etiquette.title: Follow your host
etiquette.text: At a home or community table, wait for the host’s cue on hand-washing, seating, serving and whether food is shared.

etiquette.title: Spend where value stays
etiquette.text: Prefer locally owned guides, markets, producers and food businesses; avoid turning a community meal into a staged photo stop.

safety.title: Keep clean
safety.text: Wash or sanitise hands before eating and choose visibly clean preparation surfaces.

safety.title: Separate raw and cooked
safety.text: Be alert to utensils or boards shared between raw meat, seafood and ready-to-eat food.

safety.title: Cook thoroughly
safety.text: Prefer food cooked thoroughly and served hot, particularly meat, eggs and seafood.

safety.title: Use safe water
safety.text: Use safe water and raw ingredients; when uncertain, choose sealed water and fruit you can peel.
